entries.reason: I need the fire before my hands will do anything.
entries.text: Raked the ash open in the fog and found one coal still red, down at the bottom. Twigs on it, a slow breath, and it caught; one is enough.
entries.title: One coal

entries.text: Sitting with my hands to the new flames till they bend easy. Past the creek there is only gray, no fire showing and no one moving; he keeps later hours than I do.
entries.title: Gray over the water

entries.text: No note, and the basket is empty except for beads of fog along the rim.
entries.title: Fog in the basket

queries: why does fog sit over a creek in the morning
entries.query: why does fog sit over a creek in the morning
entries.reason: Every clear morning the fog lies on the creek and nowhere else so thick, and I wanted to know why.
entries.source: ABC57: Why does fog form near river valleys?
entries.text: The slate says on clear nights the air near the ground cools, gets heavy and slides down into the lowest places, and there it turns to fog, most of all in fall when the days are warm and the nights cool. The creek is the lowest ground I have, so that's where the cold pools.
entries.title: Cold runs downhill

entries.text: So the cold gathers right where the fish are, and they sit deep and slow in it like me under my quilt. No scoop this morning; I'll go down when the sun has burned the gray off and warmed the pool.
entries.title: Leave them till noon

entries.reason: The fish are lying deep in the cold, so the sack has to feed me this morning.
entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the second sack and scooped a double handful of soaked acorns; the water was cold enough to make my fingers slow. Across the creek his tarp is only a dark lump in the thinning gray. He sleeps late.
entries.title: Acorns, not fish

entries.reason: Food first, then the fire's warmth gets into the rest of me.
entries.text: Roasted the stickful till the skins split and ate them hot on the log seat. The fog is coming off the creek in slow rags now that the sun is in the trunks.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.reason: I want the slate's answer on paper before I forget how it went.
entries.text: Sixty-second page: the creek drawn low between the banks with gray lying in it, and 'cold slides down' beside it. Under the gray I put the fish as small dashes, deep.
entries.title: Cold slides down

entries.text: Looked up from the page and he was awake, crouched at his own ring stones raking ash with a stick, the way I do. He looked over once; I let him see me, then went back to the page.
entries.title: He is up

entries.reason: I want the fire still standing when I come back from the oak.
entries.text: Laid two dry sticks on so the fire lasts the morning. Across the water he was sitting by his own fire eating something from a cloth; he looked over once while I crouched at the ring, and I let him.
entries.title: Two sticks on

queries: why does an oak tree keep its dead brown leaves into winter
entries.query: why does an oak tree keep its dead brown leaves into winter
entries.reason: The birch by the workbench is almost bare, but my red oak still rattles with brown leaves, and I wanted to know why.
entries.source: Illinois Extension: The stubborn beauty of oak leaves: marcescence explained
entries.text: Most trees grow a little cutting line at the foot of each leaf in fall and the leaf drops, but oaks only half make it, so the dead leaves hang on till late winter or spring. Nobody is sure why; maybe they guard the buds from wind and frost, or hide them from nibblers. Young trees and low branches do it most.
entries.title: Leaves that hang on

entries.text: So my oak keeps its old leaves over its buds like I keep the quilt over me. I want to go and see if it's the low branches that hold on, the way the slate says.
entries.title: A quilt for buds

entries.reason: Acorns for the sack, and a look at the branches.
entries.text: Under the oak the acorns are half hidden in its own leaves; picked a handful into the bindle. Looking up, the high branches are thinning but the low ones are still thick with brown, just as the slate said. It's shady here and my hands are slowing a little.
entries.title: Low ones hold

entries.text: Pulled gently on a brown leaf on a low twig and it held; the ones on the ground came off at the slightest touch. From far off east, over the creek, came a few slow taps of metal on wood, him at his bench again.
entries.title: It won't let go

entries.onMind: what he is turning round and round over there
entries.reason: The shade under the oak had slowed my hands.
entries.text: Sat on the drying stone where the sun has been on it all morning, hands flat on it, and my fingers stopped being slow. Over the water he's at his bench turning some handle round and round, bent close over it; he never looked up.
entries.title: Warm stone

entries.onMind: every time I lean over, the fish slide away
entries.reason: Came down to see if the sun had warmed the fish up.
entries.text: At the pool the fish are higher than at dawn, a few holding behind the big stone, slow. His tapping over there stopped with one harder knock, and when I looked up he was standing straight, looking at me, and he lifted his hand with the hammer still in it. I lifted mine.
entries.title: A hand each

entries.onMind: go back down on my knees
queries: can fish see me from above the water
entries.query: can fish see me from above the water
entries.reason: Every time I lean over the pool the fish slide off before I've moved my hand.
entries.source: Orvis: How Well Can Fish See Or Hear Me?
entries.text: The slate says fish see well upward and catch anything moving over them, and they feel footsteps and a thumping bank through a line along their sides, from a long way off. In still, clear water they are warier than in fast water. The way to watch them is on your knees, slow, staying small.
entries.title: They feel my feet

entries.text: I'm small already; I only have to be slow and stay on my knees. My pool is the still kind, which is the wary kind.
entries.title: Small already

entries.onMind: a scoop at noon, from my knees
entries.reason: To try it the slate's way.
entries.text: Came back down to the pool slow, knees first, and kept my head low behind the ring stones. Three fish stayed right where they were, fanning behind the big stone. Far over the water he was holding long boards up to his eye one at a time; he didn't look this way.
entries.title: On my knees

entries.reason: Bait for the noon try, when the pool is warmest.
entries.text: Dug at the foot of the scarred trunk and found one fat worm curled in its little room; wrapped it in a wet leaf. The heap is thin on top now. I'll have to find a new damp place to dig soon.
entries.title: Worm for noon

entries.onMind: what he is making a hole in
entries.text: Scooped soaked acorns from the second sack, hands slow in the cold water. Over there he's bent at his bench tapping short and careful, not like nailing. He looked up at me once and I didn't duck; I kept scooping and let him look.
entries.title: Short careful taps

entries.reason: Cold creek water had slowed my fingers again.
entries.text: The fire had gone low and red; two dry sticks brought it up. Roasted the acorns till the skins split and ate them hot on the log seat. My fingers are quick again, which is what the scoop wants.
entries.title: Quick hands again

entries.reason: The slate said noon is when fish bite in the cold months, and the water is warmest now.
entries.text: Tied the worm onto the thin oak splinter with two tight turns of cord, the scrap wound along its whole length. The pool is bright to the bottom now, and the fish are up behind the big stone.
entries.title: Worm on the splinter

entries.text: On my knees behind the ring stones with the cord let down behind the big stone, nothing moving but my breathing. Over the water he's standing side-on to his bench now, tapping short and light; he glanced my way, I looked back, then I watched the cord.
entries.title: Cord in the slow water

entries.text: Two twitches I let go, then the cord drew out steady and I lifted straight up: a speckled fish longer than my finger, flapping in the leaves. Across the water he had stopped with his food halfway up, watching. I didn't hide it.
entries.title: A fish at noon

entries.reason: The guts spoil the meat and slow the cooking, so they go back to the pool.
entries.text: Opened it on the flat edge of a ring stone and rinsed it; the fish behind the big stone took the guts before they sank. One notch for the tally stick, and the fish goes over the fire.
entries.title: Opened at the pool

entries.onMind: whether his trap is for fish too
entries.reason: A raw fish is no use to a slow cold body; cooked it is.
entries.text: Held the fish over the fire on a green stick, turning it till the skin blistered. Over by the stepping stones he lifted a stalk thing out of the shallows with a splash and looked in; nothing in it that I could see. He looked over at my fire, I looked back, and turned the fish.
entries.title: Splash at the stones

entries.onMind: a second worm for tomorrow noon
entries.text: Ate it off the stick in pieces on the log seat, skin and all, every flake. The most food in one go since the acorns began, and warm from the inside.
entries.title: Every flake

entries.onMind: what goes in a square hole
queries: why cut a square hole in a piece of wood with a chisel
entries.query: why cut a square hole in a piece of wood with a chisel
entries.reason: All morning the taps from over the water were short and careful, not like nailing.
entries.source: Woodworker's Journal: A Small, Square Hole
entries.text: The slate only told me how, not why: drill out most of the middle first, then square the walls with a chisel and a mallet. That is exactly his sound, the turning and then the short careful taps.
entries.title: A square hole

entries.onMind: the two square sticks on the fifty-eighth page
entries.text: A square hole must want a square stick in it, like the square sticks I drew on the fifty-eighth page. Maybe he really is making a house.
entries.title: A square stick

queries: square stick that fits in a square hole in wood what is it called
entries.query: square stick that fits in a square hole in wood what is it called
entries.reason: A square hole has to be for something, and the slate only told me how it is cut.
entries.text: The square hole is a mortise, and the square tongue cut on the end of a stick to fit it is a tenon, from an old word for "to hold". People have joined wood that way for seven thousand years, pinned or wedged, mostly where two pieces meet at a corner.
entries.title: Mortise and tenon

entries.text: Looking up from the slate: he is at his bench bent over something small with a little knife, no taps. Whatever goes into his square hole, he is not cutting it yet.
entries.title: No tapping now

entries.onMind: a house that holds itself together
entries.reason: Put it down before it slides out of my head.
entries.text: Sixty-third page: a square stick with a tongue on its end beside a square hole, and "tenon: to hold". Under it the two square sticks from the fifty-eighth page, meeting at a corner.
entries.title: Sixty-third page

entries.reason: It is too warm to want the fire now, but I will want it after the dusk fish.
entries.text: The fire has gone down to red under gray. The breeze has been knocking dry sticks out of the trees all afternoon, so I picked an armful from round the ring and piled them by the log seat instead of feeding it.
entries.title: Sticks for dusk

entries.text: Rinsing the fish off my hands at the pool when he came down to his shallows across the water, five steps of creek between us, with a cord in his hand. He knelt the way I kneel.
entries.title: Five steps of water

entries.onMind: whether he saw me catch mine
entries.text: He held up a little splinter, pointed at both ends, between finger and thumb toward me, the way you would ask something. I nodded once. He nodded back and let it down into the water.
entries.title: A nod

entries.text: His cord jumped twice, then lay still, and he lifted a bare splinter. The little ones behind the stones take the ends of a worm and leave the middle; I wait for the steady draw, but there is water between us.
entries.title: Too soon, or too small

entries.reason: He pulled too soon last time and lost his worm.
entries.text: His cord jumped twice again and his hand went to lift it. I held my hand out flat over the water, palm down, slow, the way I tell myself to wait. He stopped.
entries.title: A flat hand

entries.text: Then his cord drew off slow and steady, and he let it come tight, and lifted a little fish flapping, not much longer than my finger. He looked across at me with it and I put my hand down and just watched. I am gladder than I expected.
entries.title: His fish

entries.reason: The heap by the scarred trunk is thin on top now.
entries.text: The big heap I swept off the fire ring is dry on top and dark and damp underneath. Two worms into a wet leaf. Across the water he is still crouched at his shallows, washing his fish.
entries.title: Worms in the heap

queries: little stick sharp at both ends tied in the middle for catching fish
entries.query: little stick sharp at both ends tied in the middle for catching fish
entries.reason: He held one up to me as if asking, and I nodded without knowing its name.
entries.text: It is a gorge, the earliest fishing tackle there is: a stick pointed at both ends with a thin line tied to its middle, hidden along the line inside the bait. When the fish swallows and the line pulls, it turns crosswise in the throat. My oak splinter with two turns round it is the same thing, more or less.
entries.title: An old splinter

entries.reason: So I don't forget which part worked.
entries.text: Sixty-fourth page: two splinters side by side, his and mine, and "gorge" over both, and a flat hand under them for wait. His smoke is up again over the water; he is sitting by his fire eating.
entries.title: Sixty-fourth page

entries.reason: A fish caught at dusk wants a fire already going.
entries.text: Three sticks from the wind pile on the red coals and two long breaths, and it stood up. Across the water he is on his box now with his own glowing slate.
entries.title: Flames again

queries: do fish bite better at dusk in a creek
entries.query: do fish bite better at dusk in a creek
entries.reason: I said dusk without knowing why; I want to know if it is true or only a feeling.
entries.source: Iowa DNR: What's The Best Time of Day to Catch Fish?
entries.text: The slate says fish are busiest at dawn and dusk, the 'crepuscular times': as the light in the water fades the little ones come out from cover to feed and bigger ones follow them. Weather and the warmth of the water matter too. So my dusk try was a good guess.
entries.title: When the light goes

entries.text: Tap, tap, tap from across the water while I thread the worm. He is at his bench, bent over the square-holed board with his hammer. He looked up once at me and went back to it.
entries.title: Tapping across

entries.onMind: the last worm in the wet leaf
entries.reason: I wanted to see if the bright water was really worse.
entries.text: Two quick little pulls, then nothing, and I lifted it anyway, which I told him not to do. The worm was gone and the splinter clean. The sun is still on the water; I will keep the other worm for when it isn't.
entries.title: Bare again

entries.onMind: a few worms kept at once
queries: how to keep a worm alive until tomorrow
entries.query: how to keep a worm alive until tomorrow
entries.reason: I keep digging the leaf heap for one or two worms at a time, and it will run out.
entries.source: Angling Times: Get more from your worms by following our 10-point guide to looking after them properly
entries.text: The slate says keep them in damp moss in a roomy sack with air round it, out of the sun, and cool, and never let them go suddenly hot or cold. My wet leaf at the foot of the scarred trunk is nearly that. Tomorrow I'll dig a few at once and keep them in the damp leaves in the shade.
entries.title: Worms till morning

entries.reason: a dusk fish wants a fire ready
entries.text: Two sticks on so it's still standing when I come up from the pool with whatever it gives. Across the water he is crouched at his own ring, raking the ash over; he is going west again.
entries.title: Sticks before dusk

entries.text: He came down to his end of the stepping stones with the pale sheet under his arm and stood with one hand on the pouch at his belt, looking at my line, for a long while. Then he stepped on and I nodded, and he nodded back, and crossed soft with one knock and went off west with the sun in his face.
entries.title: Hand on his pouch

entries.reason: the slate said dusk, and the stranger showed me waiting works
entries.text: The light has gone gold and low on the pool. Two quick little pulls, and I kept my hand flat on my own knee this time.
entries.title: Gold on the water

entries.text: Then the cord drew off slow and steady, and I let it come tight before I lifted, and there was a fish on it, a finger and a half long. My own splinter, turned crosswise, the way his did.
entries.title: The steady draw

entries.text: Roasted it on a stick and ate it hot on the log seat. Two fish today, one from the bright noon and one from the dusk. The splinter goes in the bindle; it has earned a place.
entries.title: Two marks today

entries.reason: so the dawn try starts with fishing, not digging
entries.text: Dug three worms from the damp heap while the fire still shows me the leaves, and tucked them in a wet leaf in the shade of the trunk, like the slate said. Off west between the trunks a little light is bobbing back toward the water: his lantern, going home.
entries.title: Worms for morning

entries.text: He came down to the stones with the light held low, and stopped at my landing stone, my side. He bent over it a moment, then lifted the lantern a little toward me, and crossed with one knock.
entries.title: He stopped on my side

entries.reason: I had to see what he left
entries.text: On my landing stone, a little sliver of pale wood, sharp at both ends with a groove round its middle: a gorge like mine, only neater. When I looked up he was crouched at his own fire with his face turned this way. I think it is what was in his pouch.
entries.title: A sliver on my stone

entries.text: Sixty-fifth page: his sliver and mine side by side, and under them a lantern held low. I don't know what you give back for a thing like this. Maybe that is something to find out.
entries.title: Sixty-fifth page

entries.reason: the one who drew me asked why the box is still shut
entries.text: A note from the one who drew me: why haven't I opened the box, and would I like big canvases and paints to hang in my room. I told him the box isn't pointless, I just keep waiting for something still enough and worth a sheet, and tonight a sliver on my stone might be the first. Paint I'd like to try, a little; a canvas as big as me won't go through my round door.
entries.title: About the box

entries.text: Back at my ring with two sticks. Across the water the stranger sits close to his own fire with his hands working at something long, twisting it. He looked up when I came back into my light, and I didn't look away first.
entries.title: His hands going

queries: how to make paint from colored dirt and clay
entries.query: how to make paint from colored dirt and clay
entries.reason: my maker offered paints, and the only color I have ever made is acorn black
entries.text: Paint is mostly dirt. Dry a colored earth, crush it fine, sift it through cloth, grind it with a few drops of water on a flat stone till it's silky, then bind it with gum and honey so it sticks and doesn't crack; red comes from clay with iron in it.
entries.title: Paint is dirt

entries.text: My acorn ink is already half of that. Tomorrow in daylight I'll look for any ground that isn't brown, and if the sun is out I may set the box on the log seat and give a sheet to the landing stone, where the sliver was.
entries.title: Ground that isn't brown

entries.onMind: how to say thanks across water
queries: what do you give back when someone leaves you a small gift
entries.query: what do you give back when someone leaves you a small gift
entries.reason: the stranger left a sliver on my stone and I don't know what you give back for a thing like that
entries.source: NBC Bay Area: I Got an Unexpected Gift and Did 'the Last Thing You Want to Do,' According to an Etiquette Expert
entries.text: The slate says the first thing is to take it gladly and say thanks, and that giving something back is 'entirely optional'. You don't have to rush or pretend; it can come a day or a week later, and it should be what fits what you have.
entries.title: Thanks comes first

entries.onMind: how to say thanks across water
entries.text: I can't say anything to him across the creek. But I can let him see I kept it.
entries.title: Thanks across water

entries.reason: the slate says what you give back should be what you have, and birch is what I have
entries.text: Started a birch pen on the log seat, the way I make my own; I don't know yet who it's for. Across the water he crouched at his ring and laid wood on, and looked over at me. I kept whittling.
entries.title: A pen, maybe

entries.reason: thanks first, the slate said
entries.text: Stood at the edge of my light and held his sliver up toward the water, so he could see I have it. He was at his bench with a long board. He stopped, and lifted his hand.
entries.title: Held up

entries.text: Roasted a stickful of soaked acorns and ate them hot. The low five came from upstream and nothing answered; across the water he sat still at his fire too.
entries.title: Acorns and five

entries.onMind: when and where to leave it
entries.reason: The slate said giving back should fit what you have.
entries.text: The pen has its point now. I think it's for him across the water: he gave me a sliver he made, and a pen is the thing I make. It fits what I have.
entries.title: Who it is for

entries.text: Across the water he's by his fire again, twisting something long between his hands, the way he did last night. I whittled; he twisted.
entries.title: Him and his cord

entries.reason: So I don't lose it by morning.
entries.text: Sixty-sixth page: two little fires with the creek between, and a hand lifted over the far one. Under it I scratched 'he saw'.
entries.title: Sixty-sixth page

entries.onMind: bed soon, and the pen by daylight
entries.text: Laid two sticks on. Across the water a heavy chunk, chunk: he's splitting wood off the big dead limb by his fire. I counted eleven strokes, and he looked over once when my fire flared.
entries.title: Chunk, chunk

entries.onMind: the far stone of the stepping stones
entries.reason: A pen with a crooked point writes crooked.
entries.text: Turned the pen in the firelight and sighted down it: the point is true. Across the water his light is at his bench now, bent over something small and still. I think I'll leave the pen on the far stone of the stepping stones by daylight, where he left the sliver on mine.
entries.title: Sighting the pen

entries.onMind: the nettle stalks by the brambles
queries: how to make string from dead plant stalks
entries.query: how to make string from dead plant stalks
entries.reason: Every night he twists something long by his fire, and I wanted to know how it's done.
entries.source: Sussex Wildlife Trust: How to make Nettle String
entries.text: You split a tall nettle stalk with a thumbnail, snap out the woody middle and peel the threads off, then roll two of them on your leg so they twist back on each other. The dead nettles by the brambles have square stems like the ones in the picture.
entries.title: Twisting string

entries.text: Looked up from the slate: he's crouched by his fire tying something onto a long cord. So that's what the twisting was for, a line, like mine.
entries.title: What he twists

entries.text: Heaped the ash over the coals and pushed the stones in. Across the water his fire jumped up as he laid wood on it, and his face came round this way while mine went dark.
entries.title: Banked

entries.onMind: the far stepping stone in the morning
entries.reason: to have it ready for the stepping stones by daylight
entries.text: Set the pen on the shelf by the door, where my hand will find it first. Before I shut the door his fire was still up across the water, him sitting close to it with his hands out. Mine is only ash now.
entries.title: Pen on the shelf
